questions.q: Why do secrets scanning, SAST, and dependency scanning run before the build stage?
options: Because they are the least important checks
Because they are cheap, source-level checks that don't require a built artifact, catching problems before a more expensive build happens
Because the build stage always fails otherwise
Because CI/CD tools require this exact order by law
questions.explain: Running the cheaper, source-level checks first means a build that was already going to fail gets caught before the more expensive build and image-scan stages run on it.

questions.q: What does the image scan stage check that the earlier stages do not?
options: The developer's commit message
Vulnerable packages baked into the actual built container image layers
The policy gate's own configuration
The identity's permission list
questions.explain: Image scanning runs after the container is built specifically to catch vulnerabilities in the image layers themselves, which source-level scans can't see.

questions.q: Which of these is a precise, implementable policy gate rule, as described in this lesson?
options: "Fail if anything looks bad"
"Block the deploy if the secrets scan finds any match, or if SAST/dependency scan reports CVSS 9.0+, or if the image scan reports an unexcluded critical finding"
"Block the deploy whenever a developer disagrees with a finding"
"Never block a deploy, just log a warning"
questions.explain: A vague rule like 'fail if anything looks bad' can't actually be implemented. The precise rule names specific, checkable conditions tied to each scan's output.

questions.q: In the least-privilege identity definition for order-service-deploy, what permissions are granted?
options: Full subscription owner access
Read access to its own two Key Vault secrets, write access to its own logs, and deploy access to its own container environment — nothing else
Read access to every service's secrets in the organization
No permissions at all, since the pipeline handles deployment automatically
questions.explain: The identity is defined explicitly with exactly three permissions scoped to order-service's own resources — nothing broader is listed, so nothing broader is granted.

questions.q: What problem from the kickoff scenario does the explicit identity definition in this lesson directly fix?
options: Slow build times
The broad, never-revisited deploy identity that had accumulated more access than order-service actually needed
A missing SAST configuration
An expired TLS certificate
questions.explain: Lesson 29 described order-service's starting identity as broadly scoped and never revisited. Explicitly naming only the three needed permissions is the concrete fix for that accumulated over-privilege.
